Pathology-02.question: ১) “Break-bone fever” is suggestive of?
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is dengue fever. Dengue is classically known as “break-bone fever” because of the severe myalgia, arthralgia, and bone pain experienced by patients.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Lyme disease – Associated with erythema migrans rash and arthritis due to Borrelia burgdorferi.

  • Relapsing fever – Characterized by recurrent episodes of fever due to Borrelia species.

  • Typhoid fever – Causes prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms, and relative bradycardia.

High-yield points:

Dengue fever:

  • Cause → Dengue virus (Flavivirus)

  • Vector → Aedes mosquito

  • Features:

    • High fever

    • Severe myalgia (“break-bone” pain)

    • Retro-orbital pain

    • Thrombocytopenia

    • Rash

Exam pearl:
Break-bone fever = Dengue fever.

Pathology-02.question: ২) Which of the following is the commonest physical finding in enteric fever?
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is coated tongue. A coated tongue is one of the common physical findings in enteric (typhoid) fever due to systemic infection and dehydration.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Abdominal tenderness – May occur, but is less common and not the most frequent physical finding.

  • Rose spots – A classic sign of typhoid fever, but occur in only a minority of patients.

  • Hepatosplenomegaly – May occur but is not the commonest finding.

High-yield points:

Enteric fever features:

  • Sustained fever

  • Relative bradycardia (Faget sign)

  • Coated tongue

  • Abdominal discomfort

  • Hepatosplenomegaly (occasionally)

  • Rose spots (classically described but uncommon)

Exam pearl:
Most common physical finding in enteric fever = coated tongue.

Pathology-02.question: ৩) Which of the following is not a presentation of tertiary syphilis ?
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is condylomata lata. It is a feature of secondary syphilis, not tertiary syphilis.

Syphilis stages:

  • Primary syphilis

    • Painless chancre at the site of inoculation

  • Secondary syphilis

    • Generalized rash (including palms and soles)

    • Condylomata lata

    • Lymphadenopathy

  • Tertiary syphilis

    • Gumma formation

    • Cardiovascular syphilis (e.g., aortitis, aneurysm)

    • Symptomatic neurosyphilis (e.g., tabes dorsalis, general paresis)

High-yield points:

Stage Key features
Primary Chancre
Secondary Condylomata lata, rash
Tertiary Gumma + cardiovascular + neurosyphilis

Exam pearl:
Condylomata lata = secondary syphilis; gumma = tertiary syphilis.

Pathology-02.question: ৪) Campylobacter jejuni infection have been linked to
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). Infection with Campylobacter jejuni is the most common infectious trigger associated with GBS.

Mechanism:

  • C. jejuni lipooligosaccharide (LOS) mimics peripheral nerve gangliosides

  • Immune cross-reaction → demyelination/axonal injury of peripheral nerves

  • Causes ascending flaccid paralysis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gas gangrene – Mainly caused by Clostridium perfringens.

  • Myocarditis – Commonly associated with viruses such as Coxsackie B.

  • Inflammatory bowel disease – Not a recognized classic association with C. jejuni.

High-yield points:

Campylobacter jejuni:

  • Causes → Acute inflammatory diarrhoea

  • Complication → Guillain–Barré syndrome

  • Also associated with reactive arthritis

Exam pearl:
Campylobacter jejuni → GBS (classic post-infectious complication).

Pathology-02.question: ৫) Infections that can be used as bioterrorism
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Bacillus anthracis. It is a well-known bioterrorism agent because of its:

  • Ability to form resistant spores

  • Long environmental survival

  • Potential for aerosol dissemination

  • High mortality in inhalational anthrax

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) – Can cause severe disease and has been considered a potential biothreat agent, but is not the classic answer.

  • Nocardiosis – Opportunistic infection, not a recognized major bioterrorism agent.

  • Actinomyces – Causes chronic suppurative infections but is not used as a bioterrorism agent.

High-yield points:

Category A bioterrorism agents (CDC):

  • Bacillus anthracis → Anthrax

  • Yersinia pestis → Plague

  • Francisella tularensis → Tularemia

  • Variola virus → Smallpox

  • Botulinum toxin (Clostridium botulinum)

  • Viral haemorrhagic fever viruses

Exam pearl:
Anthrax = classic bioterrorism organism.

Pathology-02.question: ৬) Dysentery is caused by
৭) Chronic carrier state of typhoid fever lies in
৮) Common clinical features of syphilitic chancre
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is shallow and punched out ulcer. A primary syphilitic chancre is classically:

  • Single

  • Painless

  • Clean-based

  • Shallow, punched-out ulcer

  • Associated with non-tender regional lymphadenopathy

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bleeding on touch – Not a typical feature of a syphilitic chancre.

  • Multiple ulcer – Primary chancre is usually solitary.

  • Painful ulcer – Suggests chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) rather than syphilis.

High-yield points:

Disease Ulcer feature
Syphilis (chancre) Painless, clean, punched-out ulcer
Chancroid Painful, ragged ulcer
Herpes genitalis Multiple painful vesicles/ulcers

Exam pearl:
Syphilitic chancre = painless, solitary, punched-out ulcer.

Pathology-02.question: ৯) Atypical pneumonia is caused by all of the following except
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Haemophilus influenzae. It is a typical cause of typical bacterial pneumonia, producing a lobar pneumonia pattern with:

  • Acute onset fever

  • Productive cough

  • Focal chest signs

  • Lobar consolidation

The other options are associated with atypical pneumonia:

  • Adenovirus – Can cause viral atypical pneumonia.

  • Influenza virus – Causes viral pneumonia with atypical features.

  • Chlamydia pneumoniae – Causes atypical pneumonia with dry cough and systemic symptoms.

High-yield points:

Common causes of atypical pneumonia:

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae

  • Chlamydia pneumoniae

  • Legionella pneumophila

  • Viruses (influenza, adenovirus, RSV)

Typical pneumonia organisms:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae

  • Haemophilus influenzae

  • Staphylococcus aureus

  • Gram-negative bacilli

Exam pearl:
Atypical pneumonia = Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella, viruses; H. influenzae = typical.

Pathology-02.question: ১০) Swarming growth in blood agar media found for-
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Proteus. Proteus species show characteristic swarming growth on blood agar, where bacteria spread across the agar surface in concentric waves due to their highly motile peritrichous flagella.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Klebsiella – Non-motile, produces large mucoid colonies due to capsule.

  • Legionella – Requires special media (BCYE agar) and does not show swarming.

  • Vibrio – Motile with polar flagella but does not show swarming growth.

High-yield points:

Proteus:

  • Swarming growth on blood agar

  • Urease positive

  • H₂S positive (P. mirabilis)

  • Causes UTI and struvite stones

Exam pearl:
Swarming motility on blood agar = Proteus.

Pathology-02.question: ১১) Most common cause of nosocomial diarrhoea-
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Clostridium difficile. It is the most common cause of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) diarrhoea, especially after:

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotic use (e.g., clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones)

  • Disruption of normal gut flora

It causes:

  • Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea

  • Pseudomembranous colitis due to toxin A and toxin B

The other options are incorrect because:

  • E. coli – Common cause of community-acquired diarrhoea but not the leading nosocomial cause.

  • Entamoeba – Causes amoebic dysentery, usually community-acquired.

  • Shigella – Causes bacillary dysentery, not the commonest hospital-acquired diarrhoea.

High-yield points:

Clostridium difficile:

  • Gram-positive, anaerobic spore-forming bacillus

  • Risk factor → Antibiotics

  • Toxins → A (enterotoxin) + B (cytotoxin)

  • Disease → Pseudomembranous colitis

Exam pearl:
Nosocomial diarrhoea after antibiotics = Clostridium difficile.

Pathology-02.question: ১২) Main agent in necrotizing fasciitis-
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Streptococcus. The main agent of necrotizing fasciitis is Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).

It causes rapidly progressive infection of:

  • Deep fascia

  • Subcutaneous tissue

  • Skin

Associated features:

  • Severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings

  • Fever and systemic toxicity

  • Tissue necrosis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Staphylococcus – Can be involved, especially in polymicrobial infections, but is not the classic main agent.

  • Vibrio – Vibrio vulnificus can cause necrotizing wound infections, especially in liver disease, but is less common.

  • Lactobacillus – Normal flora; not a cause of necrotizing fasciitis.

High-yield points:

Necrotizing fasciitis:

  • Classic organism → Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes)

  • Also called → “flesh-eating disease”

  • Requires urgent surgical debridement + antibiotics

Exam pearl:
Necrotizing fasciitis = Group A Streptococcus.

Pathology-02.question: ১৩) Which chemical structure is septic shock inducer?
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is lipopolysaccharide (LPS). LPS is a component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and acts as an endotoxin that can induce septic shock.

Mechanism:

  • LPS (especially lipid A) activates macrophages

  • Release of inflammatory cytokines:

    • TNF-α

    • IL-1

    • IL-6

  • Leads to systemic inflammation, vasodilatation, hypotension, and septic shock

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Peptidoglycan – A bacterial cell wall component, but not the major endotoxin causing septic shock.

  • Ribosome – Responsible for protein synthesis; not involved in endotoxin activity.

  • Mesosome – An outdated bacterial structure concept; not a septic shock mediator.

High-yield points:

LPS = Endotoxin

  • Found in → Gram-negative bacteria

  • Toxic component → Lipid A

  • Effect → Septic shock

Exam pearl:
Gram-negative septic shock is mainly due to Lipid A of LPS.

Pathology-02.question: ১৪) Site of infection for Campylobacter jejuni
১৫) Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by
১৬) Kaposi’s sarcoma is caused by
১৭) Predisposing factor for toxic shock syndrome
১৮) Endocarditis on prosthetic heart valve is caused by
১৯) UTI in young women is mostly caused by
২০) Which streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis & meningitis?
২১) Which organism causes endocarditis following dental procedure?
২২) Spores germinate in reheated rice
২৩) Which clostridium causes gas gangrene?
২৪) Dysentery is caused by
২৫) The obligate intracellular bacteria –
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Rickettsia prowazekii. Rickettsia species are obligate intracellular bacteria because they depend on host cells for energy production and replication.

  • R. prowazekii → Epidemic typhus

  • Transmitted by → Body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Legionella pneumophila – Facultative intracellular organism that replicates inside macrophages but can grow on special media (BCYE agar).

  • Mycobacterium leprae – An intracellular pathogen causing leprosy, but not classified as an obligate intracellular bacterium.

  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae – Lacks a cell wall and is not intracellular; causes atypical pneumonia.

High-yield points:

Obligate intracellular bacteria:

  • Rickettsia

  • Chlamydia

Exam pearl:
Rickettsia = obligate intracellular bacteria.

Pathology-02.question: ২৬) Non capsular Organisms -
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Cryptosporidium spp. It is a non-capsulated protozoan parasite that causes diarrhoea, especially in immunocompromised patients.

The other options are incorrect because they are encapsulated organisms:

  • Haemophilus influenzae – Has a polysaccharide capsule (especially type b, Hib).

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae – Has a prominent polysaccharide capsule (important virulence factor).

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae – Has a large polysaccharide capsule, causing mucoid colonies.

High-yield points:

Encapsulated organisms (important for exams):

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae

  • Haemophilus influenzae type b

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae

  • Neisseria meningitidis

  • Cryptococcus neoformans

Exam pearl:
Among the options, Cryptosporidium is the non-capsulated organism.

Pathology-02.question: ২৭) Diseases caused by viridans streptococcus
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is endocarditis. Viridans streptococci are normal flora of the oral cavity and are a classic cause of subacute infective endocarditis, especially after dental procedures in patients with abnormal heart valves.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Erysipelas – Usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus).

  • Scalded skin syndrome – Caused by Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxin.

  • Toxic shock syndrome – Classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus (TSST-1 toxin).

High-yield points:

Organism Disease
Viridans streptococci Subacute infective endocarditis
S. pyogenes Erysipelas, rheumatic fever
S. aureus TSS, scalded skin syndrome

Exam pearl:
Viridans streptococcus = dental flora + subacute endocarditis.

Pathology-02.question: ২৮) Staphylococcus aureus causes the following toxin mediated diseases
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is scalded skin syndrome. Staphylococcus aureus causes toxin-mediated disease through production of specific exotoxins.

  • Scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) → caused by exfoliative toxin (exfoliatin) of S. aureus

  • Food poisoning (gastroenteritis) → caused by preformed enterotoxin of S. aureus (also toxin-mediated)

Among the given options, scalded skin syndrome is the best answer.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Scarlet fever – Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin.

  • Acute rheumatic fever – A post-streptococcal immune complication after S. pyogenes infection, not toxin-mediated.

High-yield points:

Toxin-mediated diseases of S. aureus:

  • Scalded skin syndrome → Exfoliative toxin

  • Toxic shock syndrome → TSST-1

  • Food poisoning → Enterotoxin

Exam pearl:
S. aureus exfoliative toxin = Scalded skin syndrome.

Pathology-02.question: ২৯) Pseudomembranous enterocolitis is caused by-
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Clostridium difficile. It causes pseudomembranous enterocolitis, typically following antibiotic therapy that disrupts normal intestinal flora.

Mechanism:

  • Produces toxins:

    • Toxin A (enterotoxin) → intestinal fluid secretion and inflammation

    • Toxin B (cytotoxin) → mucosal damage and cell death

  • Forms characteristic pseudomembranes in the colon

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Clostridium botulinum – Causes botulism due to neurotoxin.

  • Streptococcus faecalis (Enterococcus faecalis) – Causes UTI, endocarditis, and biliary infections.

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Causes hospital-acquired infections, pneumonia, and wound infections; not pseudomembranous colitis.

High-yield points:

C. difficile:

  • Risk factor → Broad-spectrum antibiotics (especially clindamycin)

  • Disease → Pseudomembranous colitis

  • Toxins → A + B

Exam pearl:
Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea with pseudomembrane = Clostridium difficile.

Pathology-02.question: ৩০) Non-Specific antibody tests for syphilis are
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test). It is a non-specific (non-treponemal) antibody test used for screening and monitoring treatment response in syphilis.

It detects antibodies against cardiolipin-lecithin-cholesterol antigen, not antibodies directly against Treponema pallidum.

The other options are incorrect because they are specific treponemal tests:

  • TPHA – Treponemal test (detects antibodies against T. pallidum).

  • TPPA – Treponemal test.

  • FTA-ABS – Treponemal test with high specificity.

High-yield points:

Non-treponemal tests:

  • VDRL

  • RPR

  • Used for:

    • Screening

    • Monitoring treatment response (titres fall after successful therapy)

Treponemal tests:

  • TPHA

  • TPPA

  • FTA-ABS

Exam pearl:
VDRL/RPR = non-specific; TPHA/TPPA/FTA-ABS = specific for syphilis.

Pathology-02.question: ৩১) Chronic carrier state of typhoid fever lies in
৩২) Shape of Vibrio cholera
৩৩) Which one remains positive for life in syphilis?
৩৪) Vertical transmission occurs in case of-
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is toxoplasmosis. Vertical transmission (mother-to-child transmission) is a classic feature of congenital toxoplasmosis.

Transmission:

  • Pregnant woman acquires primary infection with Toxoplasma gondii

  • Parasite crosses the placenta

  • Causes congenital infection

Features of congenital toxoplasmosis:

  • Chorioretinitis

  • Hydrocephalus

  • Intracranial calcifications

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Malaria – Can rarely cross the placenta and cause congenital malaria, but it is not the classic exam association.

  • Dracunculosis – Transmitted by contaminated water containing infected copepods.

  • Hepatitis A virus (HAV) – Mainly transmitted by the faeco-oral route; vertical transmission is very rare.

High-yield points:

TORCH infections (vertical transmission):

  • T → Toxoplasma gondii

  • O → Other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19)

  • R → Rubella

  • C → Cytomegalovirus

  • H → Herpes simplex virus

Exam pearl:
Congenital infection + chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus = Toxoplasmosis.

Pathology-02.question: ৩৫) Fibre optic instrument is best sterilized by
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is glutaraldehyde. Fibre optic instruments (e.g., endoscopes) cannot tolerate high temperatures, so they are sterilized using cold chemical sterilization methods.

Glutaraldehyde (2%) is widely used for:

  • High-level disinfection

  • Sterilization of heat-sensitive medical equipment

  • Fibre optic instruments

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 70% ethanol – Effective antiseptic/disinfectant but not a reliable sterilizing agent because it does not destroy all spores.

  • Lysol – Used as a disinfectant but not suitable for sterilizing delicate instruments.

  • Phenol – Disinfectant; not used for sterilization of fibre optic instruments.

High-yield points:

Heat-sensitive instruments → chemical sterilization:

  • 2% Glutaraldehyde

  • Ethylene oxide gas

  • Hydrogen peroxide plasma

Exam pearl:
Fibre optic endoscope = glutaraldehyde sterilization.

Pathology-02.question: ৩৬) Normal Flora of vagina maintained by
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is oestrogen. Vaginal normal flora, mainly Lactobacillus (Döderlein bacilli), is maintained by oestrogen.

Mechanism:

  • Oestrogen stimulates vaginal epithelial cells to store glycogen

  • Lactobacillus converts glycogen to lactic acid

  • Maintains acidic vaginal pH (~3.8–4.5)

  • Prevents growth of pathogenic organisms

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Progesterone – Important in maintaining pregnancy but does not maintain vaginal acidity.

  • DCP (dicalcium phosphate) – Not involved in vaginal flora regulation.

  • Prostaglandin – Involved in inflammation and uterine contraction, not normal vaginal flora.

High-yield points:

Normal vaginal flora:

  • Organism → Lactobacillus (Döderlein bacillus)

  • Maintained by → Oestrogen

  • Mechanism → Glycogen → Lactic acid → Acidic pH

Exam pearl:
Oestrogen maintains Lactobacillus and acidic vaginal environment.

Pathology-02.question: ৩৭) Endospore formation is seen in
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is Clostridium difficile. It is a spore-forming, Gram-positive anaerobic bacillus.

Endospores help C. difficile to:

  • Survive in the environment for long periods

  • Resist disinfectants

  • Spread in hospitals

The other options are incorrect because they do not form endospores:

  • Brucella melitensis – Gram-negative coccobacillus causing brucellosis.

  • Coxiella burnetii – Intracellular Gram-negative organism causing Q fever; does not form true bacterial endospores.

  • Bacteroides fragilis – Anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus; non-spore forming.

High-yield points:

Spore-forming bacteria:

  • Bacillus species → aerobic Gram-positive rods

    • B. anthracis

    • B. cereus

  • Clostridium species → anaerobic Gram-positive rods

    • C. tetani

    • C. botulinum

    • C. perfringens

    • C. difficile

Exam pearl:
Endospore formation = Bacillus + Clostridium.

Pathology-02.question: ৩৮) Heat sensitive surgical instruments are sterilized by
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is ethylene oxide gas and glutaraldehyde solution. Heat-sensitive surgical instruments cannot withstand autoclaving or dry heat, so they are sterilized by low-temperature methods.

Examples:

  • Ethylene oxide (ETO) gas → sterilizes plastic, electronic, and delicate surgical equipment

  • Glutaraldehyde solution → high-level disinfection/sterilization of heat-sensitive instruments (e.g., fibre optic endoscopes)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hot air oven – Uses dry heat and requires high temperature; suitable for glassware and metal instruments.

  • Ionizing radiation – Used mainly for industrial sterilization of disposable medical supplies.

  • Absolute alcohol – Disinfectant, not a sterilizing agent; ineffective against spores.

High-yield points:

Heat-sensitive instruments →

  • Ethylene oxide gas

  • Glutaraldehyde

  • Hydrogen peroxide plasma

Heat-stable instruments →

  • Autoclave

  • Hot air oven

Exam pearl:
Heat-sensitive surgical instruments = ETO gas + glutaraldehyde.

Pathology-02.question: ৩৯) Bacterial zoonotic diseases -
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is plague. It is a classic bacterial zoonotic disease caused by Yersinia pestis.

Transmission:

  • Reservoir → Rodents (especially rats)

  • Vector → Flea (Xenopsylla cheopis)

  • Humans acquire infection through flea bites

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Shigellosis – Human-to-human transmission via faeco-oral route; no important animal reservoir.

  • Typhoid fever – Caused by Salmonella Typhi; humans are the main reservoir.

  • Cholera – Caused by Vibrio cholerae; associated with contaminated water and seafood, not classically zoonotic.

High-yield points:

Important bacterial zoonoses:

  • Yersinia pestis → Plague

  • Brucella spp. → Brucellosis

  • Bacillus anthracis → Anthrax

  • Leptospira spp. → Leptospirosis

Exam pearl:
Rodent + flea + bubonic plague = zoonotic bacterial disease.

Pathology-02.question: ৪০) Pathogenesis of dengue shock syndrome
৪১) Saddle back fever
৪২) Which streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis & meningitis?
৪৩) Which organism causes endocarditis following dental procedure?
৪৪) Which clostridium causes gas gangrene?
৪৫) RNA nucleocapsid virus
৪৬) Kaposi’s sarcoma is recurrent infection of
৪৭) Initial site of infection of VZV in
৪৮) Antigenic shift & drift occurs in
৪৯) Negri bodies are found in
৫০) Common organisms of meningitis in neonate include
Pathology-02.exp:
The correct answer is E. coli. In neonatal meningitis, the common causative organisms include:

  • Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)

  • Escherichia coli (especially K1 strain)

  • Listeria monocytogenes

Among the given options, E. coli is the classic neonatal meningitis organism.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Staphylococcus epidermidis – Mainly associated with catheter-related infections and prosthetic device infections.

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae – Can cause neonatal sepsis, especially in hospital settings, but is not the classic common organism.

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa – Causes healthcare-associated infections but is not a common cause of neonatal meningitis.

High-yield points:

Neonatal meningitis (0–28 days):

  • GBS (S. agalactiae)

  • E. coli (K1 antigen)

  • Listeria monocytogenes

Exam pearl:
Neonate + meningitis = GBS, E. coli K1, Listeria.
